title: Suðuroy & Mykines: Faroese Isolation Week

bestPeriod.window: **Mid-May to late August** — the Mykines ferry and the puffin colony operate only in this window. September gives the clearest air and the emptiest villages but Mykines access closes

accommodation.note: €100–180 per night for a guesthouse or a self-catering house; village houses rented whole from €130

food.note: €45–75 per day; self-catering is near-obligatory outside Tvøroyri and Vágur

transport.note: €350–500: flights, the Suðuroy ferry (2 h), the Mykines ferry, and a hire car

summary: A seven-day nature escapes & cabin stay itinerary in Suðuroy (southernmost island) and Mykines (westernmost island), Faroe Islands.

itinerary.title: Tórshavn and the Smyril ferry to Suðuroy
itinerary.morning: Arrive Vágar, drive to Tórshavn, buy a week of food — the supermarkets in the capital are far better stocked than anything in the south.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Smyril ferry** from Tórshavn to Tvøroyri takes about two hours across open water. Take the car; Suðuroy has no other way to move.
itinerary.evening: Tvøroyri, a town strung along a fjord with a black wooden church moved here from Norway in the 18th century. Settle in.

itinerary.title: The west coast cliffs: Beinisvørð and Sumba
itinerary.morning: Drive south to **Beinisvørð**, a 470 m sheer cliff face dropping into the Atlantic — the most imposing sea cliff on the island and reachable by a short walk from the road.
itinerary.afternoon: Sumba, the southernmost village, and Akraberg lighthouse beyond it at the island's tip, where the next land south is Scotland. Wind here is a physical force.
itinerary.evening: Village house or Vágur guesthouse. There is no restaurant in most of these settlements: cook.

itinerary.title: Fámjin and Hvannhagi
itinerary.morning: **Fámjin**, reached over a mountain road, is a village of perhaps thirty houses on the west coast. Its church holds the original **Merkið**, the Faroese flag, sewn by students in 1919.
itinerary.afternoon: The **Hvannhagi** hike from Tvøroyri — a hanging valley of boulders and small lakes with a view to the island of Lítla Dímun, the smallest of the eighteen islands and the only uninhabited one. About three hours return, steep, and stunning.
itinerary.evening: Long light, no traffic, nothing scheduled.

itinerary.title: Vágur, Ásmundarstakkur and the bird cliffs
itinerary.morning: Vágur, the island's second town, and the walk out to **Ásmundarstakkur**, a sea stack with a natural arch, on a headland covered in nesting seabirds.
itinerary.afternoon: The eastern coast road and the abandoned village sites; Suðuroy has lost population steadily for a century, and the empty houses are part of the landscape.
itinerary.evening: If you have arranged one, a **heimablídni** dinner in a Suðuroy home — the island's version is warmer and less commercial than the capital's.

itinerary.title: Ferry back and reposition to Vágar
itinerary.morning: The Smyril back to Tórshavn, then west to Sørvágur on Vágar.
itinerary.afternoon: Prepare for Mykines: check the ferry status, pack for a night with everything you need, including all food.
itinerary.evening: Sørvágur. Early night — the Mykines boat goes early and decisions get made at first light.

itinerary.title: Mykines
itinerary.morning: The **Mykines ferry** from Sørvágur takes about 45 minutes and runs only in the summer season. It cancels frequently in swell. Landing at the village jetty involves a steep climb up steps from the boat.
itinerary.afternoon: The walk out along the ridge to **Mykineshólmur**, over a footbridge above a chasm, to the lighthouse and the **gannet colony** — the only one in the Faroes. The path passes through dense puffin burrows; a hiking fee applies and a guide may be required on parts of the route. `verify: true`
itinerary.evening: Stay overnight in the village guesthouse if you can get it. When the day boat leaves, Mykines has perhaps a dozen people on it and the silence is total.

itinerary.title: Return and departure
itinerary.morning: The morning boat back — or the helicopter, if the sea is up and you have a seat.
itinerary.afternoon: Vágar airport is twenty minutes from Sørvágur. Build slack: a Mykines cancellation can strand you a day, and this is the known risk of the itinerary.

accommodationStrategy.name: Whole-house rentals in Suðuroy villages
accommodationStrategy.description: Faroese families rent out village houses — turf roof, thick walls, a kitchen, sometimes a hot tub facing the Atlantic. €110–180 for the house. This is level-2 isolation: no shop, no restaurant, no traffic, and the best value on the islands.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Bakkin / Tvøroyri and Vágur guesthouses
accommodationStrategy.description: The practical bases with a restaurant, a shop and fuel. Choose one of these for the first and last Suðuroy nights and a village house in between.

accommodationStrategy.name: Mykines guesthouse
accommodationStrategy.description: A handful of beds on an island of ten residents, with meals cooked by your host because there is no alternative. It books out for the entire summer within weeks of opening. If you want one night of genuine North Atlantic isolation, this is it — and it requires planning months ahead.

logistics.emergency: 112. Suðuroy has a hospital in Tvøroyri; Mykines has nothing, and evacuation is by boat or helicopter and weather-dependent. This is a genuine consideration for anyone with a medical condition.
logistics.weather: Wind is the operating variable. Above roughly 15 m/s, boats stop, cliff walks become dangerous and mountain roads close. Cliff edges here are unfenced, wet, and grassed — the classic accident is a slip on a 35° grass slope above a 400 m drop.
logistics.bookingWindows: Mykines guesthouse: as soon as the season opens, 6+ months. Suðuroy village houses: 2–3 months. Cars: 2–3 months for summer.

other.label: There is no right to roam
other.text: Faroese land is owned and hiking access is regulated. Several routes charge a landowner fee, some require a guide, and a few close during the sheep gathering and the bird-nesting season. Never assume a path is public. `verify: true`

other.label: Wild camping is not permitted
other.text: outside designated campsites. This is different from Norway, Sweden and Finland and catches out Nordic-experienced travellers regularly.

other.label: Ferries and cancellation
other.text: The Suðuroy ferry is large and reliable. The **Mykines ferry is small and cancels often** — plan a two-night buffer, and never book a next-morning flight after a Mykines day.

other.label: Supplies
other.text: Buy food in Tórshavn. Suðuroy's shops are adequate; Mykines has none at all. Shops close early and on Sundays.

other.label: Bird ethics
other.text: Do not walk on puffin burrows — the ground is undermined and collapses. Keep to paths, do not use drones over colonies, and give gannets and their nests wide berth.

proTips: **Stay a night on Mykines.** The day-trip crowd leaves on the afternoon boat and the island becomes what it actually is. It is the single best decision available on this itinerary and the hardest to book.

Take the **helicopter** one way if you can. The subsidised inter-island service serves Mykines and Suðuroy at a remarkably low fare for a scheduled sector, and it flies when the boats do not. Rules on tourist bookings and one-way sectors change — check the current position. `verify: true`

Suðuroy is the one island where the Faroese ferry is worth taking **with a car**. Everything else is walkable; here, distances and mountain roads make a car the difference between two villages and eight.

Ask your host about the **grindadráp** debate if you are curious about it, and listen rather than argue. It is a real and complex part of Faroese life and the visitor's confident opinion is rarely welcome.
Faroese village houses often have an outdoor **hot tub facing the sea**. Booking one in Fámjin or Sumba turns a wet, wind-blasted day into the reason you came.
Build a **spare day** into the end. Not as a luxury — as the mechanism that stops a cancelled Mykines boat from becoming a missed flight.

raw.remote_access: No 4x4 needed — roads are surfaced. The remoteness is structural: Suðuroy is a two-hour ferry from the capital with no air link, and Mykines is a small boat or a helicopter, both weather-dependent, with about ten year-round residents

isolation_levels.level_1: Tvøroyri or Vágur — small towns on Suðuroy with a shop, a bank and a restaurant
isolation_levels.level_2: A rented village house in Fámjin, Sumba or Hvalba — a handful of houses, no shop, roads that end
isolation_levels.level_3: Mykines — one settlement, no shop, no road link, ferry cancelled roughly one day in three, and total silence after the last boat leaves

raw.foraging_rules: All land in the Faroes is owned, either privately or as *útmark* commons. There is no Nordic-style right to roam: hiking off marked routes and any picking, camping or fire needs the landowner's permission. Wild camping is restricted to designated campsites
raw.wildlife: Atlantic puffin, northern gannet on Mykineshólmur, fulmar, guillemot, storm petrel; no native land mammals apart from introduced hares and mice
